object_types.name: Vendor
object_types.definition: A supplier that provides goods, services, or materials to the organization. Identified by a vendor number assigned at record creation.

source_references.excerpt: The vendor record. It's the thing in the supplier master... Legal name. Tax ID. Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong. Status. Tier. The contact.
Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.
It's the primary key. It's been the primary key since before I got here.

object_types.name: SpendTier
object_types.definition: A categorization of vendors based on spending volume. Bronze is the default tier.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a tier. Bronze, silver, gold... Gold vendors are the ones we spend real money with, they get quarterly business reviews, better payment terms, a named relationship manager.

object_types.name: RiskTier
object_types.definition: A categorization of vendors based on risk assessment from their compliance review.

source_references.excerpt: I use low, medium, high... based on the review -- what data they touch, what geography they operate in, whether they're a sole source.

object_types.name: RiskReview

source_references.excerpt: The review is its own record. It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask.

ambiguities.description: Vendor identification: TaxID is stated as non-unique due to duplicated records and parent-subsidiary arrangements, and vendor number is the system identifier. However, the transcript does not explicitly state whether any other attributes (e.g., legal name or combination of legal name + tax ID) could serve as alternative identifiers. Is tax ID reliably unique at the business rule level despite duplicates being a data quality issue, or is it truly unreliable as an identifier?

source_references.excerpt: Could you identify a vendor by tax ID instead?... You'd think so, but no. We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident and nobody's merged them... Tax ID isn't an identifier, vendor number is.

ambiguities.description: Vendor Status transition rules: The transcript discusses three statuses (draft, active, suspended) and notes that suspension can occur due to lapsed review, breach, or sanctions list. However, it does not define all valid transitions (e.g., can a draft vendor skip to suspended? Can an active vendor go back to draft? Can a suspended vendor be reactivated?). Additionally, the open item regarding in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended (run-off vs. immediate halt) affects how status transitions should be modeled.

source_references.excerpt: If we suspend a vendor -- their review lapses, or there's a breach, or they turn up on a sanctions list -- what happens to the purchase orders already in flight?... Parking it explicitly: what happens to in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Contact optionality: The model captures that a vendor can have one primary contact per region if it operates in that region. However, the transcript does not explicitly state whether a vendor MUST have a contact in every region where it operates, or whether having a contact is optional. The Meridian example implies that operating in a region without a documented contact is problematic (and resulted in a control), but the rule is not formally stated.

source_references.excerpt: And can a vendor have no contact in a region?... If they don't operate in that region, there's nothing there at all. Most of our vendors are one region only. It's the big ones that are multi-region.

ambiguities.description: Address optionality and structure: The transcript mentions that vendors can have three types of addresses (remit-to, ship-from, legal), and that these are 'frequently different and frequently wrong.' It is unclear whether a vendor must have all three address types, some subset, or whether each type is optional. Additionally, the model currently treats VendorAddress as a single text value, but the transcript's concern about errors suggests address might need to be decomposed into structured components (street, city, state, postal code, country).

source_references.excerpt: Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.

ambiguities.description: Vendor contact details optionality: The transcript lists contact attributes as 'name, email, phone number' but does not clarify whether all three are mandatory for a contact record or if some are optional. For example, can a primary contact record exist with a name but no email or phone?

source_references.excerpt: Each vendor has one primary contact. Name, email, phone number.

ambiguities.description: Risk Review sign-off status: The transcript uses the phrase 'current signed-off review' when describing the condition for active status, but the model does not capture an explicit attribute or fact type that indicates whether a review is 'signed-off' or 'current.' It is unclear whether these are separate boolean attributes on the RiskReview entity, or whether they are inferred from some other state (e.g., temporal ordering, a flag, or a workflow step). Without this clarity, the constraint 'Every active vendor has a current signed-off risk review' cannot be fully formalized.

source_references.excerpt: Every active vendor has exactly one completed risk review... A vendor accumulates review records over time. At most one is the current one. Being active requires a current signed-off review.

ambiguities.description: Spend tier assignment criteria: The transcript states that every vendor gets a spend tier with bronze as the default if nobody's assessed them, but does not define the explicit criteria or process for assigning or changing spend tier (gold, silver, bronze). Is this based on historical spending, forward projections, strategic importance, or some other metric? Is tier reassignment automatic (e.g., based on annual spend totals) or manual?

source_references.excerpt: Gold vendors are the ones we spend real money with, they get quarterly business reviews, better payment terms, a named relationship manager... We've asked people to say spend tier and risk tier. Nobody does. It's been a losing battle for two years.

ambiguities.description: PurchaseOrder amount data type: The model captures POAmount as a money type, but the transcript does not specify the currency or whether orders can span multiple currencies. Is amount always in a single, standard currency (e.g., USD), or can a PO specify multiple currencies?

source_references.excerpt: It has an amount and a raised date... I'll take vendor, number, amount, date and we can extend later.

ambiguities.description: Ternary fact type optional participation: The model 'Vendor operates in Region with Contact' requires all three roles to form a valid fact. However, the transcript's discussion of 'most vendors are one region only' and the optional nature of contacts per region leaves ambiguous whether a Vendor-Region pair MUST have an associated Contact. The earlier statement 'If they don't operate in that region, there's nothing there at all' suggests no contact record exists if the vendor doesn't operate there, but it does not explicitly require a contact when a vendor DOES operate in a region.

source_references.excerpt: it's one primary contact per region... If they don't operate in that region, there's nothing there at all. Most of our vendors are one region only. It's the big ones that are multi-region.

ambiguities.description: Region scope: The transcript mentions four regions (EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM) as 'fixed' today, with discussion of potentially splitting EMEA but no decision made. It is unclear whether the regions are truly closed to these four, or if there is a business need to add new regions in the future. Additionally, the model assumes Region is a reference entity (with region_code as identifier), but the transcript never explicitly confirms whether region codes are the only way to identify regions or if regions could be identified by names.

source_references.excerpt: Region code. EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM... Four regions, fixed?... Four today. There's been talk of splitting EMEA but it hasn't happened.

ambiguities.description: Preferred vendor flag outside model scope: The transcript reveals that Mei maintains a spreadsheet with an unofficial 'preferred' flag indicating which vendor to buy from when multiple vendors can supply the same thing. The facilitator explicitly decided not to model this as a rule because it is ad hoc and lacks defined criteria. However, this means the model is incomplete regarding a real business decision point. If the organization eventually formalizes this rule, it would require a relationship between Vendor and Product (or Commodity), plus a constraint, but this is currently out of scope.

source_references.excerpt: There's a column called 'preferred.' It means if two vendors can supply the same thing, buy from this one. It's not in the system anywhere... It's ad hoc. Don't model it.

ambiguities.description: Vendor and Contact naming conflict: Both Vendor and Contact have a Name attribute (VendorName and ContactName). The transcript does not clarify whether 'contact' is always an individual person or could represent a department or organizational entity. If Contact can represent an organizational unit, then ContactName might be misleading. Additionally, it is unclear whether a Contact can be shared across multiple vendors or whether each contact is bound to exactly one vendor.

source_references.excerpt: Each vendor has one primary contact. Name, email, phone number.
